scope: 25 whole uncertainty records inspected; exact integrated parent retention remains pending.
additional_source_basis: Earlier auxiliary full-page rereads of148/150–152,162/164–166/169–172,177–178/182–184/192/195/197 and independent current-record/source-first review.

rows.review_disposition: 151–152 confirm uncertain intended end state, contrasting claimed negotiation with suspected foreign-backed return. Preserve alternatives rather than proving a private restoration plan.
150 distinguishes public denial, authorial doubt and a British observer’s private-belief attribution. Political rise is certain; early republican conviction remains qualified.

144–146 distinguish Assembly clergy, bishops, parish clergy and later retractors. Around half/all clergy,54percent/parish clergy and perhaps10percent/retractions are different denominators/times, not contradictory interchangeable totals.
148 gives no evidence of an escape plan for Saint-Cloud and explicitly links obstruction with subsequent flight preparations. Keep confrontation and consequence, not an asserted attempted escape.
156–157 condition prompt action on other powers, while Austria privately expected none and disbanded troops. Political alarm was real despite limited operational intent; preserve that paradox.
Approximate participants/casualties/emigrant officers need their own qualifiers and denominators. Do not mechanically turn all reported counts into exact facts.
Brabant and Liège share a military context but differ institutionally. Preserve separate useful access and source-based priorities without treating the movements as equivalent.

164–165 Nootka demonstrates rejection of dynastic obligation through a concrete British-Spanish dispute. Preserve episode and principle with calibrated priorities; one cannot replace the other by label alone.
170 explicitly extends into1792. The chapter heading does not exclude eligible later-dated prose; retain dates instead of silently forcing all events into1791.
Genevan exile differs historically from Dutch and Belgian refugees. Optional distinct access can preserve that difference without over-weighting a brief example.
162 gives Pro Aris et Focis organizational and Church-funding roles before armed exile intervention. Consolidation must retain those mechanisms and avoid saying the name is merely decorative.

171 Gustavus is an explicit exception to monarchical reluctance; his concentrated treatment has real comparative value. Retain the exception rather than using length to erase it;197 assassination remains a distinct subsequent phase.
160/172 separate Clootz’s enthusiasm from staged international delegation and genuine exile advocacy. Preserve both the theatrical element and actual political hopes.
173 treats cheap annexation of Avignon as a defiant diplomatic gesture amid army weakness. Earlier papal/civil conflicts remain distinct and cannot be replaced by this short retrospective statement.
Ownership of157–158 is administrative, not a semantic uncertainty. Retire this completion assertion; actual Pillnitz/Avignon content remains governed by substantive requirements.

182–183 explicitly make the southern movement’s meaning difficult to determine while suggesting defensive anti-feudal motivation. Keep the qualified explanation alongside rumor, local polarization and government weakness.
178/180/191/194–195 terminology develops from war advocates into loose Convention circles. Linked routes are appropriate, but no fixed party roster or timeless synonymy follows.

190–192 separate Marat’s advocacy, Danton’s searches/intervention saving intended arrestees, Commune coordination and later partisan blame. Preserve roles and Longwy-before-search versus Verdun-before-massacre chronology.
Related Brissotin/Girondin names preserve evolving political roles. The later loose grouping is not a modern disciplined party retrospectively present at every earlier action.
184 alleged Austrian Committee language is political accusation; actual royal correspondence/war hopes are separate evidence. Do not prove a formal conspiracy committee from hostile rhetoric.
191 states Commune involvement in coordinating, not stopping, massacres and circulating provincial hints. This is substantive responsibility but not evidence of one prior comprehensive order.
191–192 contrast perpetrators’ fears of prison conspirators with victims mostly not politically dangerous/common criminals. Preserve belief versus authorial assessment.

192 says killing seemed to reassure sansculottes about family safety before mass volunteering. Replace opaque first-formulation shorthand with that qualified causal observation; neither moral endorsement nor a proven necessary cause of military success follows.
196 says fear perhaps swayed some death votes; preserve this modal and the separate death/delay/reprieve divisions. Do not claim crowd pressure dictated every deputy’s choice.

183 links violence to feared reversal of anti-feudal gains while saying war did most to make destruction irreversible. Retain reinforcing war/local mechanisms rather than falsely making war precede all attacks.
